## Project summary

### Project title and location

The proposed project, **Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan**, will support the fictional coastal city of Harbor Point to reduce exposure to extreme heat and street flooding between 2027 and 2032. The plan was adopted by the Harbor Point City Council on 14 March 2026 and serves a city with 182,400 residents.

[Information needed: Confirm the country in which Harbor Point is located for the GCF SAP proposal.]

### Delivery arrangements

The Office of Climate Resilience will lead delivery in partnership with the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works will deliver green stormwater infrastructure; the Harbor Point Unified School District will host schoolyard conversions; and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance will co-design cool-corridor routes with residents.

[Information needed: Confirm the GCF-accredited entity that will submit and oversee the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal.]

### Scope, duration and financing

The project will deliver 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors in Eastside and Millbrook, 85 bioretention cells, 3.2 hectares of permeable green schoolyard play areas, and 18 community cooling centres.

The total programme cost is USD 26.5 million. Harbor Point will contribute USD 7.9 million from its capital budget, while USD 18.6 million is sought in external grant funding. The planned implementation period is 2027–2032.

[Information needed: Confirm the amount of GCF grant funding requested for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan and whether it comprises the full USD 18.6 million external grant requirement.]

## Climate rationale and baseline

Harbor Point faces compound climate-related risks from extreme heat and stormwater flooding. The proposed Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan addresses these risks between 2027 and 2032 through urban greening, green stormwater infrastructure and community cooling measures.

### Extreme heat

Harbor Point recorded 23 days above 35 °C in 2025, compared with an average of 9 such days per year during 1991–2020. Heat-related emergency department visits increased from 140 in 2021 to 310 in 2025.

Eastside and Millbrook have the city’s lowest tree-canopy cover, at 11 percent and 13 percent respectively.

### Stormwater flooding

Street flooding affects 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event. The Canal Street underpass closed six times in 2025 because of standing water. In Eastside, the existing drainage network was designed for a 5-year storm and is undersized for current rainfall intensities.

### Exposed population and assets

Harbor Point has 182,400 residents. The cool corridors are planned in Eastside and Millbrook, which have the lowest tree canopy in the city, and Eastside’s drainage network is undersized for current rainfall intensities. Documented flood exposure includes 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event and the Canal Street underpass.

[Information needed: Confirm the number and characteristics of people exposed to extreme heat and stormwater flooding in Eastside and Millbrook, including any priority groups to be targeted by the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Baseline conditions and need for intervention

The project responds to documented heat and flooding conditions through an integrated package of measures. The baseline includes low tree-canopy cover in Eastside and Millbrook, recurring heat-related emergency department visits, flood-prone intersections, and drainage infrastructure that is inadequate for current rainfall intensities. These conditions provide the rationale for increasing shade and canopy, improving local rainwater capture, and making cooling facilities available during days above 32 °C.

## Project components and activities

The Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan will implement an integrated package of urban greening, green stormwater infrastructure and community cooling measures between 2027 and 2032.

### Component 1: Cool corridors

The project will plant 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors connecting schools, clinics and transit stops in Eastside and Millbrook. Activities will include tree planting and three years of establishment watering. The intended outcome is to increase tree canopy cover in both neighbourhoods to 25 percent by 2032.

Cool-corridor planting and establishment watering are estimated to cost USD 9.6 million.

### Component 2: Green stormwater infrastructure

The project will construct 85 bioretention cells and convert 3.2 hectares of asphalt schoolyards into permeable green play areas. Together, these measures are designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface.

Green stormwater infrastructure activities will include design and construction supervision and are estimated to cost USD 14.2 million.

[Information needed: Confirm the locations of the 85 bioretention cells and the schoolyards to be converted into 3.2 hectares of permeable green play areas under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Component 3: Community cooling network

The Office of Climate Resilience will designate 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres. These centres will have extended opening hours on days above 32 °C to provide accessible cooling facilities during extreme-heat conditions.

The community cooling network is estimated to cost USD 2.7 million and is funded from the city operating budget.

[Information needed: Confirm the locations of the 18 libraries and recreation centres to be designated as community cooling centres under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Delivery roles

The Office of Climate Resilience will lead delivery together with the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works will deliver the green stormwater infrastructure component; the Harbor Point Unified School District will host schoolyard conversions; and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance will co-design cool-corridor routes with residents.

## Expected results and indicators

### Expected adaptation results

The Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan is intended to reduce exposure to extreme heat and street flooding between 2027 and 2032. Expected results include increased shade and urban tree canopy along routes connecting schools, clinics and transit stops; improved local capture of rainfall from impervious surfaces; and accessible cooling facilities during days above 32 °C.

The project will deliver 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors, 85 bioretention cells, 3.2 hectares of permeable green schoolyard play areas, and 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres. The green stormwater measures are designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface.

### Beneficiaries

The cool corridors serve Eastside and Millbrook, where tree-canopy cover is currently 11 percent and 13 percent respectively, and where Eastside’s drainage network is undersized for current rainfall intensities. The cool corridors connect schools, clinics and transit stops, and the 18 community cooling centres are located in libraries and recreation centres.

[Information needed: Confirm the number of direct and indirect beneficiaries of the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan in Eastside and Millbrook, disaggregated by relevant priority groups where available.]

### Indicators, baselines and targets

| Result area | Indicator | Baseline | Target by 2032 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Urban heat resilience | Tree-canopy cover in Eastside | 11 percent | 25 percent |
| Urban heat resilience | Tree-canopy cover in Millbrook | 13 percent | 25 percent |
| Cool-corridor delivery | Street trees planted along cool corridors | Not stated | 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors |
| Green stormwater delivery | Bioretention cells constructed | Not stated | 85 bioretention cells |
| Green stormwater delivery | Asphalt schoolyards converted to permeable green play areas | Not stated | 3.2 hectares |
| Green stormwater performance | Impervious surface served by measures designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall | Not stated | 41 hectares |
| Community cooling access | Community cooling centres designated | Not stated | 18 centres with extended opening hours on days above 32 °C |
| Flooding resilience | Flooded intersections during monitored storms | Street flooding affects 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event | [Information needed: Confirm the target reduction in flooded intersections during monitored storms that the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan will achieve by 2032.] |
| Heat-health resilience | Heat-related emergency department visits | 310 visits in 2025, up from 140 in 2021 | [Information needed: Confirm the 2032 target for heat-related emergency department visits to be used for monitoring the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.] |

### Monitoring and reporting

The Office of Climate Resilience will publish an annual progress report. Monitoring will include tree-canopy cover, the number of flooded intersections during monitored storms, and heat-related emergency department visits.

## Implementation arrangements

### Implementing entities and partner roles

The Office of Climate Resilience will lead delivery together with the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works will deliver the green stormwater infrastructure component, including the planned bioretention cells and permeable green schoolyard play areas.

The Harbor Point Unified School District will host schoolyard conversions. Millbrook Neighbours Alliance will co-design cool-corridor routes with residents. The Office of Climate Resilience will designate 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres, with extended opening hours on days above 32 °C.

### GCF-accredited entity and governance

[Information needed: Confirm the GCF-accredited entity that will submit, oversee and provide fiduciary management for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal.]

The Harbor Point City Council adopted the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan on 14 March 2026. The Office of Climate Resilience and the Department of Public Works will lead project delivery, with delivery roles for the Harbor Point Unified School District and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance as described above.

[Information needed: Confirm the governance structure for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan, including the body that will make implementation decisions, its membership, meeting frequency, and escalation arrangements between the Office of Climate Resilience, Department of Public Works, Harbor Point Unified School District and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance.]

### Monitoring, reporting and learning

The Office of Climate Resilience will publish an annual progress report. Monitoring will include tree-canopy cover, the number of flooded intersections during monitored storms, and heat-related emergency department visits.

[Information needed: Confirm the monitoring and reporting protocol for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan, including data owners, collection methods and frequency, quality assurance, reporting recipients, and the process for acting on monitoring findings.]

## Indicative financing

### Cost basis and total programme cost

The Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan has an indicative total programme cost of USD 26.5 million. This cost is based on the following component estimates:

| Component | Indicative cost (USD million) | Cost basis |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Cool corridors | 9.6 | Planting 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors and three years of establishment watering |
| Green stormwater infrastructure | 14.2 | Construction of 85 bioretention cells and conversion of 3.2 hectares of asphalt schoolyards into permeable green play areas, including design and construction supervision |
| Community cooling network | 2.7 | 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres with extended opening hours on days above 32 °C |
| **Total** | **26.5** | **Integrated heat and stormwater resilience programme** |

### Co-financing

Harbor Point will contribute USD 7.9 million from its capital budget. The community cooling network, estimated at USD 2.7 million, is identified as funded from the city operating budget.

[Information needed: Confirm how the USD 7.9 million Harbor Point capital-budget contribution and the USD 2.7 million city operating-budget funding for the community cooling network are allocated across the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan components, and confirm whether the operating-budget funding is included within the USD 7.9 million contribution.]

### GCF funding request and financial instrument

The plan seeks USD 18.6 million in external grant funding. The cool-corridor and green stormwater infrastructure components are identified as seeking grant funding.

[Information needed: Confirm the amount of GCF funding requested for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal, whether it will cover the full USD 18.6 million external grant requirement, and the amount allocated to each project component.]

[Information needed: Confirm the proposed GCF financial instrument for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal, including whether the request is entirely a grant and any terms or conditions that apply.]

### Financing consistency

The component financing status identifies both cool corridors (USD 9.6 million) and green stormwater infrastructure (USD 14.2 million) as seeking grant funding, while the overall external grant requirement is stated as USD 18.6 million.

[Information needed: Reconcile the USD 18.6 million external grant requirement with the financing status of the USD 9.6 million cool-corridor and USD 14.2 million green stormwater infrastructure components, and confirm the final financing plan for each component of the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

Open gap question: Confirm the country in which Harbor Point is located for the GCF SAP proposal.
Why asking: The GCF SAP proposal must identify the project’s city and country to establish the eligible national context and location of proposed activities.

Open gap question: Confirm the GCF-accredited entity that will submit and oversee the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal.
Why asking: A GCF SAP proposal requires an accredited entity with responsibility for submission, fiduciary oversight, and implementation supervision.

Open gap question: Confirm the amount of GCF grant funding requested for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan and whether it comprises the full USD 18.6 million external grant requirement.
Why asking: The proposal must distinguish the GCF funding request from total project cost, municipal co-financing, and any other external financing.

Open gap question: Confirm the number and characteristics of people exposed to extreme heat and stormwater flooding in Eastside and Millbrook, including any priority groups to be targeted by the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.
Why asking: The GCF SAP proposal must demonstrate who is exposed and how the proposed measures will target vulnerable beneficiaries in the priority neighbourhoods.

Open gap question: Confirm the locations of the 85 bioretention cells and the schoolyards to be converted into 3.2 hectares of permeable green play areas under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.
Why asking: The GCF SAP proposal requires quantified outputs and their locations; the plan provides quantities but does not identify the sites for these green stormwater investments.

Open gap question: Confirm the locations of the 18 libraries and recreation centres to be designated as community cooling centres under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.
Why asking: The GCF SAP proposal must identify the locations of the proposed community cooling assets and confirm where extreme-heat service delivery will occur.

Open gap question: Confirm the number of direct and indirect beneficiaries of the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan in Eastside and Millbrook, disaggregated by relevant priority groups where available.
Why asking: The GCF SAP proposal requires a substantiated beneficiary statement and needs beneficiary numbers and priority-group reach to demonstrate the scale and equity of expected adaptation benefits.

Open gap question: Confirm the target reduction in flooded intersections during monitored storms that the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan will achieve by 2032.
Why asking: A quantified target is needed to assess whether the green stormwater component will reduce the documented baseline of flooding at 37 intersections.

Open gap question: Confirm the 2032 target for heat-related emergency department visits to be used for monitoring the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.
Why asking: A defined target is needed to measure the plan’s intended heat-health outcome against the 2025 baseline of 310 heat-related emergency department visits.

Open gap question: Confirm the GCF-accredited entity that will submit, oversee and provide fiduciary management for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal.
Why asking: A GCF SAP proposal must identify the accredited entity responsible for submission, fiduciary oversight and accountability to GCF.

Open gap question: Confirm the governance structure for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan, including the body that will make implementation decisions, its membership, meeting frequency, and escalation arrangements between the Office of Climate Resilience, Department of Public Works, Harbor Point Unified School District and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance.
Why asking: The proposal must demonstrate how cross-agency delivery decisions, coordination and issue escalation will be governed.

Open gap question: Confirm the monitoring and reporting protocol for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan, including data owners, collection methods and frequency, quality assurance, reporting recipients, and the process for acting on monitoring findings.
Why asking: Indicator results and the annual progress report cannot be considered reliable or usable for adaptive management without defined data and reporting responsibilities.

Open gap question: Confirm how the USD 7.9 million Harbor Point capital-budget contribution and the USD 2.7 million city operating-budget funding for the community cooling network are allocated across the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan components, and confirm whether the operating-budget funding is included within the USD 7.9 million contribution.
Why asking: The co-financing total and component-level financing plan cannot be confirmed without establishing whether these city funding amounts are additional or overlapping.

Open gap question: Confirm the amount of GCF funding requested for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal, whether it will cover the full USD 18.6 million external grant requirement, and the amount allocated to each project component.
Why asking: The SAP financing section must distinguish the GCF request from other external funding and show how requested funds finance the proposed components.

Open gap question: Confirm the proposed GCF financial instrument for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal, including whether the request is entirely a grant and any terms or conditions that apply.
Why asking: The financial instrument determines how the requested GCF funding can be presented and whether repayment or other financing obligations must be reflected.

Open gap question: Reconcile the USD 18.6 million external grant requirement with the financing status of the USD 9.6 million cool-corridor and USD 14.2 million green stormwater infrastructure components, and confirm the final financing plan for each component of the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.
Why asking: The stated grant requirement is inconsistent with the components identified as seeking grant funding, so the total funding need and component financing cannot yet be verified.
